lead: OpenGL is a standard application programming interface (API) for drawing 2D and 3D graphics. A program describes shapes once, and the same calls run on many graphics cards. OpenGL behaves as a state machine: settings stay until you change them, and vertices move through the pipeline stages until they become coloured fragments in a framebuffer. Games, CAD tools and phone map apps rely on it. Only a few universities teach this depth.
prereq: You need: raster scan displays and RGB colour.

blocks.text: OpenGL is a library of function calls for drawing. Your program calls it; the graphics driver turns those calls into commands for the GPU. It does not open a window or read image files; a toolkit such as GLFW or GLUT does that.

A context holds the state for one window and one thread. It stores the current colour, line width, bound buffers, active shader program and viewport. Create the context first; every later call acts on it.
The viewport is the pixel rectangle inside the window where the picture appears. glViewport(x, y, width, height) sets it, in pixels, with the origin at the bottom-left.

OpenGL is a state machine because these settings persist. glColor3f(1, 0, 0) sets red; every vertex drawn after it is red until another colour call. That saves calls but causes bugs: state set for one object silently colours the next.
Vertices enter at the top and leave as pixels. Each stage has one job.

items: Vertex fetch reads attributes such as position, colour and normal from GPU buffers.
Vertex shader runs once per vertex and outputs the clip-space position.
Primitive assembly groups vertices into points, lines or triangles.
Clipping cuts geometry outside the view volume and adds new vertices at the boundary.
Rasterizer finds the pixels each primitive covers and makes one fragment per covered pixel.
Fragment shader runs per fragment and returns its colour; the depth value is interpolated from the vertices by the rasterizer.
Depth and stencil tests accept or reject a fragment; blending then merges the accepted colour with what is already in the framebuffer.
Framebuffer stores the surviving colour and depth values.

blocks.text: The figure shows six of these eight stages, leaving out clipping and the per-fragment tests for space. The rasterizer is the hinge: before it, geometry in floating-point coordinates; after it, fragments that carry interpolated colour and depth. Several fragments may map to one screen pixel; the depth test keeps the nearest. Fragments rejected at the tests never touch the framebuffer.

Modern OpenGL (version 3.2 and later, core profile) removed fixed-function drawing. The old style, glBegin(GL_TRIANGLES) … glVertex3f(x, y, z) … glEnd(), sent one vertex per call and is deprecated; old tutorial code no longer runs.

Now vertices sit in a vertex buffer object (VBO) in GPU memory, and a vertex array object (VAO) records the attribute layout and which buffer each attribute comes from. Shaders are small programs in GLSL, compiled and linked at run time into a program object.

Double buffering keeps the picture steady. The front buffer is what the screen shows; you draw into the back buffer, then swap them, typically once per refresh (60 Hz). Without a swap you see an unfinished frame; without clearing the back buffer, old frames smear into new ones.

figure.caption: The worked example's triangle inside the 200 × 200 pixel viewport, with vertices (0,0), (200,0) and (0,200). Its area of ½ × 200 × 200 = 20,000 px² is about how many fragments reach the fragment shader, one per covered pixel.

spec.aria: A right triangle plotted in a 200 by 200 pixel viewport with vertices at the origin, at 200 on the x axis and at 200 on the y axis, covering about 20,000 pixels, so about 20,000 fragments are generated.

examples.question: A triangle has vertices (0,0), (1,0) and (0,1) in a coordinate range that already covers the viewport from 0 to 1. A simple scale maps them to a 200 × 200 pixel viewport: x_screen = 200x and y_screen = 200y. Find the screen vertices and estimate the fragment count.
steps: The input coordinates already run from 0 to 1, so the simple scale by 200 maps each vertex: (0,0) → (0,0), (1,0) → (200,0), (0,1) → (0,200), all in pixels. This example uses a simple scale, not the general normalised-device-coordinate (NDC) to window mapping, because NDC runs from −1 to +1.
The shape is a right triangle with legs 200 px and 200 px.
One fragment is produced per covered pixel, so about 20,000 fragments reach the fragment shader.
examples.answer: The screen vertices are (0,0), (200,0) and (0,200) pixels, covering about 20,000 fragments.
examples.check:
w = 200
h = 200
print(w)
print(h)
print(int(0.5 * w * h))

traps: OpenGL does not draw in world coordinates: the vertex shader and viewport transform first. glVertex3f(1,0,0) is not pixel (1,0).
State persists. Colour, line width and bound buffers stay until changed, so one object's settings leak into the next.
glBegin and glEnd are missing from the core profile; old tutorial programs fail on current drivers.
A fragment is not a pixel. Several fragments can cover one pixel, and the depth test keeps only one.
Swapping is not drawing. Without a swap you see one buffer only; without clearing the back buffer you see trails.

quiz.q: Which stage turns primitives into fragments?
What does an OpenGL context hold?
quiz.a: The state and data for one window and thread: colour, viewport, buffers, shader program.

quiz.q: Why is OpenGL called a state machine?
quiz.a: Settings persist after a call and apply to every later draw until changed, so the order of calls matters.
It sends one vertex per function call, so the driver handles millions of small calls per frame instead of one buffer upload.

quiz.q: A 400 × 300 viewport shows a triangle covering half its area. How many fragments appear?
A frame flickers while being drawn. Which change fixes it and why?
quiz.a: Draw into the back buffer and swap after the frame is complete; the front buffer then always shows a finished frame.

beyond: Not for the exam. On the job, OpenGL is one of several APIs; Vulkan, Metal and WebGL expose the same pipeline with different control. Shaders now do general computation (GPGPU) as well as colour. Search "OpenGL core profile", "GLSL", and "Vulkan pipeline" to go further.
